name: Aridai
title: Son of Haman, killed in Susa
summary: Aridai was one of the ten sons of Haman, the Agagite, who was the declared enemy of the Jews during Persian rule. He is named in the book of Esther among the sons who fell when the Jews were granted the right to defend themselves against those who sought their lives. King Ahasverus gave the Jews this right after Queen Esther revealed Haman's conspiracy. The killing of Aridai and his brothers marked the final reckoning with the threat posed by Haman’s family, and these events form the historical basis for the annual Purim festival in Jewish tradition.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Plan to Destroy the Jews
keyEvents.description: Haman, father of Aridai, devised a plan to destroy all the Jews in the Persian Empire, which directly affected Haman's entire family.

keyEvents.title: The Fall of Haman
keyEvents.description: After Queen Esther revealed Haman's evil plot to King Ahasuerus, Haman was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai.

keyEvents.title: The Jews' Right to Self-Defense
keyEvents.description: King Ahasuerus issued a new decree granting the Jews the right to defend themselves against their enemies, which proved fateful for Haman's sons.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Ten Sons Are Killed
keyEvents.description: Aridai was killed along with his nine brothers when the Jews defended themselves against their enemies in the capital city of Susa. All ten of Haman's sons fell.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Sons Are Hanged
keyEvents.description: At Queen Esther's request, King Ahasuerus ordered that the bodies of Haman's ten sons, including Aridai, be hanged as a public example.

keyEvents.title: The Feast of Purim Is Established
keyEvents.description: After the victory over Haman's family and the enemies of the Jews, the feast of Purim was established as an annual celebration to commemorate the deliverance of the Jewish people.

versions.summary: Aridai was one of the ten sons of Haman the Agagite, who was an enemy of the Jewish people in Persia. He was killed along with his brothers when the Jews defended themselves against their enemies after King Ahasuerus gave them permission to protect themselves. His death marked the end of Haman's family's attempt to destroy the Jewish people.
versions.title: Son of Haman
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Son of Haman' is correct, but could be made slightly more descriptive by including context from the book of Esther.; [major] There is no biblical support for Aridai being a 'warrior'. He is mentioned solely as one of Haman's sons who was killed. The role should be changed to something more neutral, such as 'son of Haman' or similar.; [minor] The events in the book of Esther are usually dated to around 480–470 BC under Xerxes I (Ahasuerus). '400s BC' is acceptable but could be specified somewhat.; [minor] The summary is good, but it is worth noting that Haman is called an 'Agagite' (not an 'Amalekite') in the Hebrew text. The term 'Agagite' may indicate a connection to the Amalekites, but the biblical term should be used.; [major] Footnotes are missing. The profile should include notes on the meaning of the Hebrew name, Haman's designation as an 'Agagite', the possible link to the Amalekites, and the historical context of the Purim celebration.; [minor] The event 'The institution of the Feast of Purim' is interesting context but has only indirect connection to Aridai personally. Nevertheless, it is reasonable to include it as background.

versions.title: Son of Haman, killed in Susa
versions.reason: [minor] The title is fine, but 'Susan' is the Norwegian form. Some prefer 'Susa', but 'Susan' is also common in Norwegian Bible translations, so this is acceptable.; [minor] The summary is well phrased and theologically correct. It correctly uses 'Agagite' instead of 'Amalekite' and provides good context. No changes needed.; [minor] There are many key events for a relatively peripheral person. The events 'Haman's plan' and 'Haman's fall' primarily concern Haman, not Aridai directly. Nevertheless, they provide important context, so this is acceptable.

footnotes.text: The name Aridai (Hebrew: אֲרִידַי) is likely of Persian origin. Many scholars have attempted to link it to Old Iranian word forms, but a definitive etymology is difficult to establish. The fact that Haman's sons bear Persian names reflects the Persian context in the book of Esther.

Haman is described in the Hebrew text as 'the Agagite' (ha-Agagi). This title is traditionally linked to Agag, king of the Amalekites whom Saul spared (1 Sam 15). Rabbinic tradition views the conflict between Mordecai (of the tribe of Benjamin) and Haman as a continuation of the ancient conflict between Israel and Amalek (cf. Exod 17:8-16 and Deut 25:17-19).

In Jewish tradition, the names of Haman's ten sons in Esther 9:7-9 are read in one long breath during the liturgical reading of the Scroll of Esther (Megillat Esther) at Purim, to emphasize that they all died simultaneously. This tradition is recorded in the Talmud (Megillah 16b).

The events in the book of Esther are usually placed under the Persian king Xerxes I (486–465 BC), identified with Ahasuerus. The capital Susa is well documented archaeologically, and the famous palace at Susa has been the subject of extensive excavations since the 19th century, confirming the magnificent architecture described in the book of Esther.

The hanging of Haman's sons' bodies after their death was a form of public shaming known in the ancient Near East. It was not an execution method in itself, but a demonstration of victory and deterrence, parallel to practices described in other contemporary sources from the Persian Empire.

In the Hebrew text of Esther 9:7-9, the names of Haman's ten sons are written in a special list format with extra spaces, which is unique among Hebrew biblical manuscripts. Three letters in the list are written in smaller size (zayin, shin, and tav), a feature that has been the subject of much rabbinic speculation and has been linked, among other things, to the numerical value 5707 in the Jewish calendar, corresponding to the year 1946.
